Police brutality disciplinary hearing exposed

By: Viewfinder | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we go inside the disciplinary proceedings that SAPS does not want you to see

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive (and unprecedented) access to police disciplinary hearing recordings show that unpreparedness, omission and bias by SAPS representative / evidence leader facilitated a "not guilty" finding for a police officer implicated in murdering a teenager on the Cape Flats in 2013. Watchdog case data and conflicts of interest / loopholes in police discipline management shows that what happened here is systemic.

Summary:
Damian Arendse (15) was shot and killed in Wesbank on the Cape Flats on 13 December 2013. Numerous witnesses implicated a police officer in the shooting. The police officer and his partner claimed that Damian was shot by someone else - likely the gangster whom they were chasing and shot at moments before Damian was shot. The police watchdog IPID concluded that the police officer had a murder and misconduct charge to answer for, for shooting and killing Damian. The disciplinary hearing commenced on 1 December 2014. We accessed the recording. The recording shows (in this case) what many at IPID have suspected happens on a systemic level all along - the police use these hearings to give the impression that justice is taking its course, when in fact SAPS discipline officials leading evidence can often be unprepared and biased to help facilitate "not guilty" findings against their accused colleagues. We have lifted a number of soundbites from the recordings to illustrate instances where this happened. We have now sent right of reply emails to the officer accused, and the discipline official in this case (via SAPS WC spokesperson) and request for interview with National Commissioner Khehla Sitole on the health (or ill-health) of police discipline management, and his proposals for fixing it (which he alluded to in Parliament a couple of weeks ago). We have secured Gareth Newham as an expert to comment on how police discipline management is flawed in South Africa.

Further information:
None, all is contained above.

Script:


Script
Behind closed doors: inside the police disciplinary hearings SAPS does not want the
public to see

Commentary 1:
From the Cape Flats to the suburbs south of Johannesburg police in South Africa stand
accused of killing hundreds of people and brutalising thousands more every year.

Link:
When disabled teenager Nateniël Julies was shot by a police officer in Eldorado Park last
year, a wave of public outrage led to swift arrests. But this is rare in South Africa, where
officers implicated in violent crimes routinely escape accountability.

Commentary 2:
Since 2012, the Independent Police Investigative Directorate has registered more than
47,000 complaints against the police. These complaints relate mostly to allegations of violent
crimes and include more than 5,000 deaths in custody and killings by police. This same case
data suggests that almost none of these cases lead to dismissals, following disciplinary
hearings.

Commentary 3:
Like many teenage boys in townships across the Cape Flats, 15-year-old Damian Ahrendse
dreamt of becoming a professional soccer player.

Klarina Reed:
Ja, this is his trophies. There you can see he was the top goalscorer of Wesbank Eagles -
Super Eagles. He told me one day he want to play for Liverpool. And I said to him, “Yes, my
child, you said mos, 'What's your dream you can achieve it' and I think you will be and you
will end up there, don't worry.

Commentary 4:
But on the evening of 13 December 2013, at the start of the school holidays, Damian was
shot and killed near his mother’s house in Wesbank. Witnesses said that a police officer had
pulled the trigger.
Damian’s older brother, Dominique Van Wyk was one of these witnesses.

Dominique Van Wyk:
Dis ‘n polisiebakkie. Hy’t stickers op, ja. Dis ‘n swart bakkie. Hy’t daar gestaan toe het die
bakkie so om gekom – so wild om gekom.
[Subtitle] He was standing there. Then the bakkie came around this way, came around wildly.
Toe skiet hy al. Toe skiet hy in die rigting waar my broertjie gestaan het.
[Subtitle] Then he shot in the direction of where my little brother was standing.

Klarina Reed:
This is the jacket that he had on. And there was a lot of blood on here. And as you can
see. This is where the bullet gets in, starts in. So this is where the bullet gets out. This hole
here where my finger points. This is where the bullet gets out.

Dominique van Wyk
Ek het hom herken want hy het my rooi Manchester baadjie aan wat ek vir hom gegee het
want dit het te klein geword vir my. Vir hom gegee. Want daai baadjie is bloed rooi.
[subtitle] I recognised him, because he had my red Manchester jacket on, that I gave to him
because it became too small for me. Gave to him. Because that jacket is very red.

Commentary 5
The docket into Damian’s killing contained two versions of the circumstances surrounding
his shooting. Police men Warrant Officer Michael Thebus and his partner Constable Adriaan Groenewald
said that they were pursuing armed suspects, when Thebus fired a warning shot in
self-defence. He speculated that one of these suspects may have been responsible for
shooting Damian. But, Dominique van Wyk and at least two other witnesses said that police had fired at
Damian. One witness suggested the teen had been caught up in the police’s pursuit of a
suspect from an earlier shooting.

Klarina Reed
Yes, he was falling right there. And I saw him. He's bleeding the blood run by his nose out.
And the blood was all lying there. He couldn't breathe. But what he actually was saying to
her, the police shot, shot him. This is where he was in Delft. By the Day Hospital Delft. I think
he was still alive. And I'm sitting and, right, another 20 minutes came, and the sister came to
me. And she said to me, “No, he isn't there anymore.” And I was crying and I was yelling
there and my daughter and my friend, she stands there, you know, and I sit there and I take
his hand and his body's already cold.

Commentary 6
In 2014, the Independent Police Investigative Directorate recommended that Lieutenant
Michael Thebus be disciplined for Damian Ahrendse’s killing. The police were legally obliged
to initiate disciplinary proceedings. But, Thebus emerged from his departmental hearing
unpunished. Why? Our access to the recordings has given us an unprecedented view into
the closed door proceedings that the South African Police Service does not want the public
to see.

Captain Gerhard van den Bergh
Die werknemer se weergawe word nie deur die werkgewer in dispuut geplaas nie.
[title] The employee’s version is not disputed by the employer (SAPS)

Captain Gerhard van den Bergh
Hy het eerlike motiewe.
[title] He has honest motives.

Commentary 7
In this hearing the police appointed Captain Gerhard Van Den Bergh. His job was to lead
evidence in an unbiased way. He supported his colleague’s claims to innocence, and
rubbished claims to the contrary.

Dominique van Wyk
Ek kan sê dis meneer Thebus, ja. Hoekom… daar’s nie ander mense wat geskiet het nie.
[title] I can say that it was Mr Thebus, yes. Why? Because there were no other people that
were shooting.

Captain Gerhard van den Bergh
… Jy’s onder ‘n wanindruk … Ek dink julle is dalk besig om die verkeerde mense te blameer.
[title] You are mistaken … I think you all are perhaps busy blaming the wrong people.

Dominique van Wyk
So eintlik, wat hulle wil doen, die polisie, is eintlik hulle wil my hele verklaring, en wat my oë
gesien het, my getuienis wil hulle eintlik minwaardig maak.
[Subtitle] What they want to do, the police, is deprecate my whole statement, that which my
eyes saw, my testimony.

Commentary 8
At the hearing, Van Wyk’s gang affiliation was used to throw his credibility into question. Yet,
Van Den Bergh did not call other witnesses who had backed up Van Wyk’s version, and had
been willing to testify.
He had placed Michael Thebus’ willingness to provide a statement in high regard.

Captain Van Den Bergh
(Dit) wys vir ons hy het eerlike motiewe.
[title] (It) shows us that he has honest motives.

Commentary 9
Thebus’ statement showed signs that he may have colluded with his partner to align their
versions. Parts of the statements were verbatim copies of one another, down to several
unusual spelling and grammar mistakes.

Commentary 10
In this statement, it appeared that Thebus had made a connection between Damian’s
Manchester United jacket and the clothing on the person upon whom he had shot. But,
during questioning, Van Den Bergh led his Thebus to omit mention of Damian’s jacket
altogether.

Captain GF Van Den Bergh
Maar die oorledene het ‘n bruin t-shirt aangehad.
[title] But, the deceased had on a brown t-shirt.
Lieutenant Michael Thebus
Dis korrek, dis wat ons gesien het.
[title] That is correct, that is what we saw.

Commentary 11
This now created the impression that Damian was not the target of Thebus’ shot.

Captain Gerhard van den Bergh
So wat jy op die oomblik vir my, wat jy op die oomblik vir ons sê dat die moontlikheid
bestaan dat hierdie laaitie wat dood is, nooit eers op die toneel was nie?
[title] So what you are telling us at this moment is there exists a possibility that the boy that
died, was never even on the scene?

Commentary 12
Finally, Van Den Bergh argued that even if Thebus had killed Damian, it would have been
justified.

Captain GF Van Den Bergh
Maar volgens die getuienis, die omstandighede, die bende aktiwiteite – sou die werknemer
se skoot, indien die werknemer se skoot die doodskoot sou gewees het, in elkgeval,
regmatiglik sou gewees het, in terme van die straf-proses wet.
[title] But, according to the witnesses, the circumstances, and the gang activity - the
employee’s shot, if indeed the employee’s shot was the fatal shot, would in any case have
been justified, in terms of the Criminal Procedure Act.

Commentary 13
Yet, an autopsy report had stated that Damian Ahrendse had been shot in the back. Van Den
Bergh did not fully explain why he believed that such a shot would have been justified.

Commentary 14
A recent investigation by journalism project Viewfinder has found that there are virtually no
checks and balances against police discipline officials overriding the findings of independent
watchdog investigations - as appears to have been the case in the disciplinary hearing for
Lieutenant Michael Thebus.

Link
There is growing consensus within government that discipline in the police service needs to
be reformed and beefed up - particularly for officers implicated in violent crimes. SAPS head
office did not respond to our request for an interview.

Commentary 15
Police in the Western Cape would not avail Michael Thebus and his former partner Adriaan
Groenewald to tell their side of the story. Spokesperson Lieutenant Colonel Andre Traut
also declined our request for an interview, because it referred to an “internal process”.

Commentary 16
Van den Bergh is no longer employed with the police. But, he defended his track record and
said his work led to the dismissal of more than 200 corrupt cops - work for which there was
apparently an attempt on his life in 2015. He did not respond to our query about his conduct
in this particular case.

Commentary 17
Gareth Newham is the Head of the Justice and Violence Prevention Programme at the
Institute for Security Studies in Pretoria.

Macfarlane Moleli
So Gareth, you obviously have been briefed on some of the findings of the investigation that
was done. Did this come as a surprise to you?

Gareth Newham
No, This did not come as a surprise to me. And it is quite consistent with my own research
on this going back to the early 2000s. Certainly there is a culture within the South African
Police Service where there is a deep reluctance amongst many police officials to do anything
that might cost their colleagues their jobs or ensure that their colleagues get sanctioned… It
just shows that routinely and systematically the disciplinary system is not working nearly as
effectively as it should… Unfortunately there’s no understanding that by not holding police
officers accountable for serious acts of criminality, brutality or other forms of ill discipline it
undermines public trust in organization and weakens the police ability to effectively promote
public safety.

Commentary 18
It has been nearly 8 years since Damian's killing. Michael Thebus has been promoted to the
rank of Lieutenant Colonel. Though the National Prosecuting Authority declined to prosecute
a murder charge, an inquest into the death has not yet been finalised. Klarina Reed remains
hopeful for justice and closure.

Macfarlane Moleli
So, what have you tried to do though to get justice for your son?

Klarina Reed
And I went to the institutions, like the government institutions ... I went to the NPA, just to ask
what happened and I phone and there’s the other one. Yeah, I went to IPID many times, I
asked the investigator, what is going on? Is there any feedback, Mr Gigi There is the court
where the dockit is lying for like months by Kuilsriver Court, it's getting dusted and all those
things. And If I phone them even, there's no answer that they give me you know, that that
make me so more hurtful, because there's no answers about my child. You know, I just want
somebody accountable for his murder. So many people tell me no you must put the photos
and stuff away. I said, no, how can I? It’s my child. He was born out of my body. He was lying
under my heart. So how can I just forget about a child because he was just a minor.


Promo 1
MacFarlane Moleli
Police disciplinary hearings happen behind closed doors. So, can these be manipulated to
protect violence accused officers from consequence? We study the tapes from one such
hearing to investigate how an officer implicated in a murder got off scot free.
Captain GF Van Den Bergh:
So wat jy op die oomblik vir my, wat jy op die oomblik vir ons sê dat die moontlikheid
bestaan dat hierdie laaitie wat dood is, nooit eers op die toneel was nie?
[title] So what you are telling us at this moment is there exists a possibility that the boy that
died, was never even on the scene?


Promo 2
Macfarlane Moleli
Last year a disabled teenager Nateniël Julies was shot and killed by police. But, he is far
from the only child killed by a trigger happy officer in recent years.
Gareth Newham:
Certainly there is a culture within the South African Police Service where there is a deep
reluctance amongst many police officials to do anything that might cost their colleagues their
jobs


Promo 3
Macfarlane Moleli:
Every year, police in South Africa stand accused of brutalising thousands of people. But,
officers implicated in these crimes are often hardly ever held accountable. With
unprecedented access to the tapes of a police disciplinary hearing for murder, we have
come one step closer to understanding why.
Dominique:
Almal praat een ding nou hier teen my, maar niemand luister vir my nie. Dit is was gebeur
het daarso.
Subtitle: Everyone is speaking against me, but no one is listening to me.” That is what
happened there.

Commentary 4: But on the evening of 13 December 2013, at the start of the school holidays, Damian was shot and killed near his mother’s house in Wesbank. Witnesses said that a police officer had pulled the trigger. Damian’s older brother, Dominique Van Wyk was one of these witnesses. Dominique Van Wyk: Dis ‘n polisiebakkie. Hy’t stickers op, ja. Dis ‘n swart bakkie. Hy’t daar gestaan toe het die bakkie so om gekom – so wild om gekom. [Subtitle] He was standing there. Then the bakkie came around this way, came around wildly. Toe skiet hy al. Toe skiet hy in die rigting waar my broertjie gestaan het. [Subtitle] Then he shot in the direction of where my little brother was standing. Klarina Reed: This is the jacket that he had on. And there was a lot of blood on here. And as you can see. This is where the bullet gets in, starts in. So this is where the bullet gets out. This hole here where my finger points. This is where the bullet gets out. Dominique van Wyk Ek het hom herken want hy het my rooi Manchester baadjie aan wat ek vir hom gegee het want dit het te klein geword vir my. Vir hom gegee. Want daai baadjie is bloed rooi. [subtitle] I recognised him, because he had my red Manchester jacket on, that I gave to him because it became too small for me. Gave to him. Because that jacket is very red. Commentary 5 The docket into Damian’s killing contained two versions of the circumstances surrounding his shooting. Police men Warrant Officer Michael Thebus and his partner Constable Adriaan Groenewald said that they were pursuing armed suspects, when Thebus fired a warning shot in self-defence. He speculated that one of these suspects may have been responsible for shooting Damian. But, Dominique van Wyk and at least two other witnesses said that police had fired at Damian. One witness suggested the teen had been caught up in the police’s pursuit of a suspect from an earlier shooting. Klarina Reed Yes, he was falling right there. And I saw him. He's bleeding the blood run by his nose out. And the blood was all lying there. He couldn't breathe. But what he actually was saying to her, the police shot, shot him. This is where he was in Delft. By the Day Hospital Delft. I think he was still alive. And I'm sitting and, right, another 20 minutes came, and the sister came to me. And she said to me, “No, he isn't there anymore.” And I was crying and I was yelling there and my daughter and my friend, she stands there, you know, and I sit there and I take his hand and his body's already cold. Commentary 6 In 2014, the Independent Police Investigative Directorate recommended that Lieutenant Michael Thebus be disciplined for Damian Ahrendse’s killing. The police were legally obliged to initiate disciplinary proceedings. But, Thebus emerged from his departmental hearing unpunished. Why? Our access to the recordings has given us an unprecedented view into the closed door proceedings that the South African Police Service does not want the public to see. Captain Gerhard van den Bergh Die werknemer se weergawe word nie deur die werkgewer in dispuut geplaas nie. [title] The employee’s version is not disputed by the employer (SAPS) Captain Gerhard van den Bergh Hy het eerlike motiewe. [title] He has honest motives. Commentary 7 In this hearing the police appointed Captain Gerhard Van Den Bergh. His job was to lead evidence in an unbiased way. He supported his colleague’s claims to innocence, and rubbished claims to the contrary. Dominique van Wyk Ek kan sê dis meneer Thebus, ja. Hoekom… daar’s nie ander mense wat geskiet het nie. [title] I can say that it was Mr Thebus, yes. Why? Because there were no other people that were shooting. Captain Gerhard van den Bergh … Jy’s onder ‘n wanindruk … Ek dink julle is dalk besig om die verkeerde mense te blameer. [title] You are mistaken … I think you all are perhaps busy blaming the wrong people. Dominique van Wyk So eintlik, wat hulle wil doen, die polisie, is eintlik hulle wil my hele verklaring, en wat my oë gesien het, my getuienis wil hulle eintlik minwaardig maak. [Subtitle] What they want to do, the police, is deprecate my whole statement, that which my eyes saw, my testimony. Commentary 8 At the hearing, Van Wyk’s gang affiliation was used to throw his credibility into question. Yet, Van Den Bergh did not call other witnesses who had backed up Van Wyk’s version, and had been willing to testify. He had placed Michael Thebus’ willingness to provide a statement in high regard. Captain Van Den Bergh (Dit) wys vir ons hy het eerlike motiewe. [title] (It) shows us that he has honest motives. Commentary 9 Thebus’ statement showed signs that he may have colluded with his partner to align their versions. Parts of the statements were verbatim copies of one another, down to several unusual spelling and grammar mistakes. Commentary 10 In this statement, it appeared that Thebus had made a connection between Damian’s Manchester United jacket and the clothing on the person upon whom he had shot. But, during questioning, Van Den Bergh led his Thebus to omit mention of Damian’s jacket altogether. Captain GF Van Den Bergh Maar die oorledene het ‘n bruin t-shirt aangehad. [title] But, the deceased had on a brown t-shirt. Lieutenant Michael Thebus Dis korrek, dis wat ons gesien het. [title] That is correct, that is what we saw. Commentary 11 This now created the impression that Damian was not the target of Thebus’ shot. Captain Gerhard van den Bergh So wat jy op die oomblik vir my, wat jy op die oomblik vir ons sê dat die moontlikheid bestaan dat hierdie laaitie wat dood is, nooit eers op die toneel was nie? [title] So what you are telling us at this moment is there exists a possibility that the boy that died, was never even on the scene? Commentary 12 Finally, Van Den Bergh argued that even if Thebus had killed Damian, it would have been justified. Captain GF Van Den Bergh Maar volgens die getuienis, die omstandighede, die bende aktiwiteite – sou die werknemer se skoot, indien die werknemer se skoot die doodskoot sou gewees het, in elkgeval, regmatiglik sou gewees het, in terme van die straf-proses wet. [title] But, according to the witnesses, the circumstances, and the gang activity - the employee’s shot, if indeed the employee’s shot was the fatal shot, would in any case have been justified, in terms of the Criminal Procedure Act. Commentary 13 Yet, an autopsy report had stated that Damian Ahrendse had been shot in the back. Van Den Bergh did not fully explain why he believed that such a shot would have been justified. Commentary 14 A recent investigation by journalism project Viewfinder has found that there are virtually no checks and balances against police discipline officials overriding the findings of independent watchdog investigations - as appears to have been the case in the disciplinary hearing for Lieutenant Michael Thebus. Link There is growing consensus within government that discipline in the police service needs to be reformed and beefed up - particularly for officers implicated in violent crimes. SAPS head office did not respond to our request for an interview. Commentary 15 Police in the Western Cape would not avail Michael Thebus and his former partner Adriaan Groenewald to tell their side of the story. Spokesperson Lieutenant Colonel Andre Traut also declined our request for an interview, because it referred to an “internal process”. Commentary 16 Van den Bergh is no longer employed with the police. But, he defended his track record and said his work led to the dismissal of more than 200 corrupt cops - work for which there was apparently an attempt on his life in 2015. He did not respond to our query about his conduct in this particular case. Commentary 17 Gareth Newham is the Head of the Justice and Violence Prevention Programme at the Institute for Security Studies in Pretoria. Macfarlane Moleli So Gareth, you obviously have been briefed on some of the findings of the investigation that was done. Did this come as a surprise to you? Gareth Newham No, This did not come as a surprise to me. And it is quite consistent with my own research on this going back to the early 2000s. Certainly there is a culture within the South African Police Service where there is a deep reluctance amongst many police officials to do anything that might cost their colleagues their jobs or ensure that their colleagues get sanctioned… It just shows that routinely and systematically the disciplinary system is not working nearly as effectively as it should… Unfortunately there’s no understanding that by not holding police officers accountable for serious acts of criminality, brutality or other forms of ill discipline it undermines public trust in organization and weakens the police ability to effectively promote public safety. Commentary 18 It has been nearly 8 years since Damian's killing. Michael Thebus has been promoted to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel. Though the National Prosecuting Authority declined to prosecute a murder charge, an inquest into the death has not yet been finalised. Klarina Reed remains hopeful for justice and closure. Macfarlane Moleli So, what have you tried to do though to get justice for your son? Klarina Reed And I went to the institutions, like the government institutions ... I went to the NPA, just to ask what happened and I phone and there’s the other one. Yeah, I went to IPID many times, I asked the investigator, what is going on? Is there any feedback, Mr Gigi There is the court where the dockit is lying for like months by Kuilsriver Court, it's getting dusted and all those things. And If I phone them even, there's no answer that they give me you know, that that make me so more hurtful, because there's no answers about my child. You know, I just want somebody accountable for his murder. So many people tell me no you must put the photos and stuff away. I said, no, how can I? It’s my child. He was born out of my body. He was lying under my heart. So how can I just forget about a child because he was just a minor. Promo 1 MacFarlane Moleli Police disciplinary hearings happen behind closed doors. So, can these be manipulated to protect violence accused officers from consequence? We study the tapes from one such hearing to investigate how an officer implicated in a murder got off scot free. Captain GF Van Den Bergh: So wat jy op die oomblik vir my, wat jy op die oomblik vir ons sê dat die moontlikheid bestaan dat hierdie laaitie wat dood is, nooit eers op die toneel was nie? [title] So what you are telling us at this moment is there exists a possibility that the boy that died, was never even on the scene? Promo 2 Macfarlane Moleli Last year a disabled teenager Nateniël Julies was shot and killed by police. But, he is far from the only child killed by a trigger happy officer in recent years. Gareth Newham: Certainly there is a culture within the South African Police Service where there is a deep reluctance amongst many police officials to do anything that might cost their colleagues their jobs Promo 3 Macfarlane Moleli: Every year, police in South Africa stand accused of brutalising thousands of people. But, officers implicated in these crimes are often hardly ever held accountable. With unprecedented access to the tapes of a police disciplinary hearing for murder, we have come one step closer to understanding why. Dominique: Almal praat een ding nou hier teen my, maar niemand luister vir my nie. Dit is was gebeur het daarso. Subtitle: Everyone is speaking against me, but no one is listening to me.” That is what happened there. ENDS

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): we go inside the disciplinary proceedings that SAPS does not want you to see
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Exclusive (and unprecedented) access to police disciplinary hearing recordings show that unpreparedness, omission and bias by SAPS representative / evidence leader facilitated a "not guilty" finding for a police officer implicated in murdering a teenager on the Cape Flats in 2013. Watchdog case data and conflicts of interest / loopholes in police discipline management shows that what happened here is systemic.
metadata.Summary: Damian Arendse (15) was shot and killed in Wesbank on the Cape Flats on 13 December 2013. Numerous witnesses implicated a police officer in the shooting. The police officer and his partner claimed that Damian was shot by someone else - likely the gangster whom they were chasing and shot at moments before Damian was shot. The police watchdog IPID concluded that the police officer had a murder and misconduct charge to answer for, for shooting and killing Damian. The disciplinary hearing commenced on 1 December 2014. We accessed the recording. The recording shows (in this case) what many at IPID have suspected happens on a systemic level all along - the police use these hearings to give the impression that justice is taking its course, when in fact SAPS discipline officials leading evidence can often be unprepared and biased to help facilitate "not guilty" findings against their accused colleagues. We have lifted a number of soundbites from the recordings to illustrate instances where this happened. We have now sent right of reply emails to the officer accused, and the discipline official in this case (via SAPS WC spokesperson) and request for interview with National Commissioner Khehla Sitole on the health (or ill-health) of police discipline management, and his proposals for fixing it (which he alluded to in Parliament a couple of weeks ago). We have secured Gareth Newham as an expert to comment on how police discipline management is flawed in South Africa.
metadata.Reason for legal: We are planning on naming people implicated directly in wrongdoing (discipline official whitewashing hearing against colleague, and police officer accused of killing someone unlawfully). We need to ensure that we don't defame them. So, yes we need a lawyer in the viewings etc.
